extracted.intended_audience: educated British political readers and legislators (18th-century public)
extracted.subtask_description: An 18th-century political pamphlet arguing standards for justice, property, religion, and historical judgment in response to the French Revolution; directed at legislators and the literate public. It sets out principles for lawful reform versus wholesale abolition and confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid collective punishment of corporate bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate bodies are immortal for the good of the members, but not for their punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not punish individuals today for the offences of their natural ancestors or for crimes associated with a corporate name; justice should target actual perpetrators, not collective genealogies or fictional pedigrees of crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use history to teach practical wisdom, not to inflame vengeance
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not draw the moral lessons we might from history. ... In the perversion, [history] may serve for a magazine, furnishing offensive and defensive weapons for parties in Church and State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply history to discern the spirit and moral quality of actions and to avoid repeating causes of evil; avoid using historical episodes as partisan weapons that revive animosities and justify revenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address causes of public evils, not merely their names or organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Wise men will apply their remedies to vices, not to names,—to the causes of evil, which are permanent, not to the occasional organs by which they act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not abolish institutions (kings, priests, magistrates, etc.) simply by changing names; reform should target enduring causes of corruption rather than destroying offices that in themselves can be beneficial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer reform over degradation or abolition of established orders
rubrics_metrics.description: If the question of this unnatural persecution is concerned, I will pay it. No one shall prevent me from being just and grateful. ... I did not find any incorrigible vices in the noblesse of France, or any abuse which could not be removed by a reform very short of abolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where abuses exist, pursue measured reform instead of wholesale abolition that degrades social orders and punishes those who do not deserve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the useful social role of nobility and privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Nobility is a graceful ornament to the civil order. It is the Corinthian capital of polished society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that honors and privileges can secure property, distinction, and social stability; excessive leveling or hasty removal of such institutions can remove valuable securities against despotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use alleged clergy vices as a pretext for general plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not with much credulity I listen to any, when they speak evil of those whom they are going to plunder. ... Vices and abuses there were undoubtedly in that order, and must be. ... But I saw no crimes in the individuals that merited confiscation of their substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism of clerical abuses must not be a cover for confiscation and persecution; investigate and punish real crimes but avoid collective confiscation based on exaggeration or malice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid legislative destruction of prescription and settled property law
rubrics_metrics.description: With the National Assembly of France possession is nothing, law and usage are nothing. I see the National Assembly openly reprobate the doctrine of prescription, which one of the greatest of their own lawyers tells us ... is a part of the law of Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uphold prescription and long-established rights; legislative revocation of prescription undermines security of property and the foundations of civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property rights against confiscation and arbitrary currency innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: They have compelled all men ... to accept, as perfect payment and good and lawful tender, the symbols of their speculations on a projected sale of their plunder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscations and forced currency (speculative symbols) destroy confidence in property and commerce; governments should not substitute fiat schemes for real, law-backed property and money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware excess public debt as a threat to political stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations are wading deeper and deeper into an ocean of boundless debt. Public debts, which at first were a security to governments, ... are likely in their excess to become the means of their subversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage public debt prudently; excessive debt can make governments odious through heavy impositions or provoke powerful discontented moneyed interests that favor new, possibly unjust regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutions of elective clergy that degrade clerical character
rubrics_metrics.description: The Assembly has provided in future an elective clergy: ... which will drive out of the clerical profession all men of sobriety ... and which will throw the whole direction of the public mind into the hands of a set of licentious, bold, crafty, factious, flattering wretches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elective processes for high ecclesiastical offices without qualifications risk reducing clerical quality, education, and independence; preserve means to secure competent and respectable clergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse toleration with indifference or contempt
rubrics_metrics.description: We hear these new teachers continually boasting of their spirit of toleration. That those persons should tolerate all opinions, who think none to be of estimation, is a matter of small merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True toleration arises from respect for justice and the value of religious truth; toleration should protect deserving religious differences, not spring from contempt or indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn fanaticism and proselytising societies that spread disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be ignorant of the spirit of atheistical fanaticism, that is inspired by a multitude of writings ... These writings and sermons have filled the populace with a black and savage atrocity of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to organized proselytism and fanatic sects whose writings and networks aim to destabilize well-governed countries and propagate discontent; such movements spread beyond borders and undermine social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use selective outrage to justify plunder
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not with much credulity I listen to any, when they speak evil of those whom they are going to plunder. An enemy is a bad witness; a robber is a worse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize motives behind denunciations; accusations that conveniently precede seizure of property are suspect and require independent verification before drastic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve middle and clerical classes to maintain learning and public virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: As with you the inferior clergy are not numerous enough for their duties ... in future nothing of science or erudition can exist in the Gallican Church.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that impoverish or demote clergy and middle ranks will drive out educated persons and erode institutional knowledge and public morality; maintain conditions that attract learned individuals to service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using theatrical or propagandistic portrayals of history to incite persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: They caused this very massacre to be acted on the stage ... Was this spectacle intended to make the Parisians abhor persecution and loathe the effusion of blood? No: it was to teach them to persecute their own pastors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about dramatizations of past crimes that are intended to inflame current passions and justify persecution; popular culture can be weaponized to mobilize violence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include commons in honors and offices to prevent aristocratic decline
rubrics_metrics.description: Those of the commons who approached to or exceeded many of the nobility in point of wealth were not fully admitted to the rank and estimation which wealth, in reason and good policy, ought to bestow ... This separation ... I conceive to be one principal cause of the destruction of the old nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow social mobility and admission of wealthy commons into suitable ranks and offices to prevent resentment and social rupture; rigid exclusion breeds instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punish real crimes but avoid degrading penalties that serve as collective punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: They were not without considerable faults and errors. ... I saw no crimes in the individuals that merited confiscation of their substance, nor those cruel insults and degradations, and that unnatural persecution, which have been substituted in the place of meliorating regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure penalties are proportional and targeted at culpable individuals; avoid punitive measures (confiscation, degradation) that collectively humiliate and dispossess entire classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain respect for legal procedures and the security of contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: We entertain a high opinion of the legislative authority; but we have never dreamt that Parliaments had any right whatever to violate property, to overrule prescription, or to force a currency of their own fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures should not cavalierly overturn settled law, prescription, or contractual rights; stability of commerce and society depends on predictable legal protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting ideological education for religion without regard for consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: These enthusiasts do not scruple to avow their opinion, that a state can subsist without any religion better than with one, and that they are able to supply the place of any good which may be in it by a project of their own ... by a sort of Civic Education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of schemes to replace religion with state-designed 'civic education' that aim to prepare minds for abolition of religion; such projects can be part of broader attempts to erode moral foundations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of toleration: genuine charity includes preference and protection
rubrics_metrics.description: They favor, therefore, and they tolerate. They tolerate, not because they despise opinions, but because they respect justice. They would reverently and affectionately protect all religions, because they love and venerate the great principle upon which they all agree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toleration should be active and protective, grounded in shared reverence for moral principles, rather than passive indifference that stems from contempt.
